subject: Technical walkthrough: where LLM requests are executed and who owns deletion
messages:
From: Ellen Park <ellen.park@edgecare.io>
To: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.com>
Cc: security@edgecare.io
Date: Sun, 12 Jul 2026 09:15:00 -0700
Subject: Quick technical Q: where do requests run / deletion responsibility?

Hi Lauren,

Thanks for the demo last week — EdgeCare is excited about Redwood's performance. Before we move to procurement, our security team asked for a simple technical note: when an LLM request hits your hosted API, which geographic regions might that request touch, which subprocessors process it (if any), and who is responsible for guaranteeing deletion when we request data erase? We mainly need: 1) path of execution across regions for hosted API, 2) any caching/kv persistence (and TTLs), 3) subprocessors that may see request metadata, and 4) deletion ownership and typical timelines.

Could you provide a short walkthrough or a diagram we can attach to our security review?

Best,
Ellen
Security Lead
EdgeCare Solutions

--
Ellen Park
security@edgecare.io

From: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.com>
To: Ellen Park <ellen.park@edgecare.io>
Cc: dev.patel@redwood.com, marissa.cole@redwood.com
Date: Sun, 12 Jul 2026 12:02:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Quick technical Q: where do requests run / deletion responsibility?

Hi Ellen,

Thanks — great questions. I pulled in Dev (Infra) and Marissa (Compliance) to make sure we capture the technical and process details. High-level summary up front:

- Execution: For Redwood hosted API, request routing is region-aware. A request from a US client is routed to our US region by default; however, routing can fall back to adjacent regions for capacity reasons unless a customer pins processing to a specific region (we support regional pinning and Private deployments).
- Subprocessors: The runtime itself runs on our cloud infra providers (we use managed GPU instances in region). Subprocessors that may see request metadata include cloud provider logging/monitoring services, the managed metrics backend, and our optional edge-cache provider (used only if enabled). We attach a CSV with the current inventory.
- Caching / KV: Short-term KV cache (model KV cache) is in-memory on the inference hosts and is ephemeral per host; prefix caching is optional and TTLs are configurable (default 0-24h for prefix cache; KV is ephemeral for the lifetime of the container). We do not write prompt text to durable object stores by default.
- Deletion: For hosted customers, customers can request account-level data erasure. We perform three steps: 1) purge customer data from indexable stores and object storage (where applicable), 2) invalidate and garbage-collect caches and KV (async; typically within 24–72 hours), 3) rotate and mark for retention removal in backups per our backup retention policy (final removal may depend on backup retention windows; typical end-to-end deletion for hosted customers is 30–90 days, depending on whether data landed in backups). For Private deployments, deletion responsibility is cooperative (customer controls primary storage).

I've attached a short diagram and our subprocessor CSV. Dev, can you add any infra-specific notes? Marissa, please confirm the backed-up retention timeline language.

Action: I'll follow up with a one-page diagram that you can put in your assessment.

Thanks,
Lauren

Subject: Re: Quick technical Q: where do requests run / deletion responsibility?

Hey Ellen — quick technical addendum from infra:

- Routing and fallbacks: Our front-end gateways prefer region-local clusters (us-west, us-east, eu-west, apac-sin). If the local cluster is saturated, the gateway will route to the nearest healthy cluster following policy (latency + cost). We can provide a hard region pin (no cross-border) for enterprise customers on Hosted with an SLA.
- Network hops: Request flow: client -> edge gateway (regional) -> auth layer (regional) -> routing service -> inference pool (GPU host in region) -> optional managed cache (if enabled) -> response. Control plane metadata (for routing and billing) is replicated across control-plane regions but request payloads are not stored in the control plane except transiently in memory and logs (logs scrubbed/hashed per retention policy).
- Subprocessors list (short): cloud-provider-x (compute + block storage) - us-west/us-east zones; metrics-provider-y (opt-in telemetry) - US/EU; edge-cache-z (optional) - deploys in region when enabled. We do not send full request text to third-party analytics by default.
- KV and model cache: model KV is process-local in GPU memory; no durable disk. Prefix cache (optional) writes to a short-lived Redis cluster (configured per customer and can be pinned to a region). If you want zero third-party visibility, we recommend disabling prefix caching and using Dedicated or Private.

Ping me if you'd like command-line examples of how to set region_pin or disable prefix cache in the Redwood API.

—Dev
Infrastructure — Redwood Inference

From: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.com>

Cc: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 13 Jul 2026 14:02:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Quick technical Q: where do requests run / deletion responsibility?

Ellen — attaching the diagram (region-exec-paths-diagram.pdf) and the subprocessor inventory CSV. A few clarifying bullets for your security packet:

- Default behavior: US client traffic stays in US regions. We do not export request payloads to non-US regions unless fallback is triggered; fallback is documented and can be disabled via region_pin.
- Evidence: For procurement we provide an evidence pack (SOC 2 summary, current subprocessor attestations). I'll ask Marissa to attach the SOC 2 excerpt and confirm deletion SLA wording.
- Deletion SLA (hosted): In typical hosted onboarding contracts we commit to initiating erasure within 48 hours and completing all non-backup removals within 30 days; final removal from backups depends on the backup window (max 90 days). We can negotiate tighter windows for enterprise commitments.

Next steps: Ellen, can you confirm whether your security team needs: 1) region-pin for all requests, 2) caching disabled by default, and/or 3) proof of subprocessor agreements? I can generate a short one-page statement for each.

Thanks,
Lauren
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
